current.lab_name: Division of Toxicology and Experimental Medicine, CSIR-Central Drug Research Institute (Lucknow, India)
current.role: Toxicologist at CSIR-CDRI in Lucknow whose group studies how organs such as the liver and lung are injured and scarred, and how hormones and drugs change that process
current.sub: Division of Toxicology and Experimental Medicine, CSIR-Central Drug Research Institute, Lucknow · also affiliated with the Academy of Scientific and Innovative Research (AcSIR)
story: Fibrosis is scarring: after repeated injury, an organ fills with stiff connective tissue and stops working well. Madhav Mugale is last author, the group leader, of a 2026 rat study on liver fibrosis caused by the toxin carbon tetrachloride (VER2026). Male rats given testosterone kept their mitochondria, the cell's power plants, in better shape, and their autophagy, the cell's recycling system, kept flowing: the protein p62 did not pile up and markers of working autophagy such as LC3B and Beclin-1 stayed higher. mTOR activity was maintained. Castrated rats did worse, with more damaged mitochondria and more cell death. The study suggests that male hormones help the liver cope with toxic injury in rats; it did not test people.

PubMed lists more than 90 papers with Mugale, all from the Division of Toxicology and Experimental Medicine at CSIR-CDRI, a national drug research institute in Lucknow, from 2019 onward. They cover safety testing of drug ingredients, models of lung and liver fibrosis, and collaborations with CDRI pharmacology groups on diabetes and insulin resistance in mice. Mugale is also affiliated with the Academy of Scientific and Innovative Research (AcSIR), which runs CSIR's doctoral programmes. No official profile page was found, so job title and training are not given.

studies.title: Testosterone propionate maintains autophagic flux and mitochondrial integrity via regulation of the LC3B/p62/Beclin-1/mTOR axis in induced liver fibrosis.

previous_note: PubMed spells the middle name both 'Nilakanth' (older papers) and 'Nilakhanth' (2026); Atlas spelling kept. Job title and training not found.

story: Songlin Li is the senior (last) author of TAO2026, which studied why largemouth bass, a carnivorous farmed fish, store too much glycogen in the liver when fed starch-rich feed. The team found that the liver's insulin-responsive mTOR/SREBP1 pathway, which would normally turn surplus sugar into fat, is impaired in this fish, so sugar is stored as glycogen instead. The result is from fish, and it adds a comparative view of how mTOR helps share out sugar between storage forms in the liver.

PubMed lists Li at Shanghai Ocean University's Research Centre on Environmental Ecology and Fish Nutrition, and at the university's National Demonstration Center on Experiment Teaching of Fisheries Science, as senior author of more than 30 papers on largemouth bass nutrition. The work tests feed ingredients and additives, such as the gut bacterium Clostridium butyricum (2023), to help fish cope with high-carbohydrate diets, and measures liver metabolism, antioxidant defences and gut bacteria.

Because Li is a very common Chinese surname, only papers with the Shanghai Ocean University fish-nutrition affiliation were counted. No official profile could be checked, so academic rank and training are not given.

studies.title: Impaired mTOR/SREBP1-Mediated Lipogenesis as a Mechanism of Hepatic Glycogen Accumulation in a Carnivorous Fish Model, Largemouth Bass (Micropterus salmoides)

current.lab_name: Bagchi Lab, Cancer Genome and Epigenetics Program, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute (La Jolla, California, USA)
current.role: Cancer geneticist at Sanford Burnham Prebys who uses chromosome engineering to find cancer genes, known for showing that MYC-amplified cancers depend on the neighbouring gene PVT1
current.sub: Lab head, Cancer Genome and Epigenetics Program (earlier Tumor Initiation and Maintenance Program), Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute (from about 2018) · University of Minnesota, Department of Genetics, Cell Biology and Development and Masonic Cancer Center (2014–2017) · Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, Alea Mills lab (2007–2008)
story: MYC is one of the most important cancer genes, and many tumours carry extra copies of it. Next to MYC on chromosome 8 sits PVT1, a gene long thought to make only non-coding RNA. The 2026 Genes and Development study found that a circular RNA made from PVT1 (circPVT1) actually carries the code for a tiny protein, which the team named Firefox (FFX). Firefox boosts AKT-mTORC1 signalling and cap-dependent translation, the main way cells make proteins, and this keeps MYC protein levels high. When Firefox was removed, MYC levels fell and MYC-amplified tumours grew less in mice carrying human cancer cells (xenografts). It points to an mTORC1-linked weak spot in MYC-driven cancers, shown in cells and mouse models.

Anindya Bagchi is the senior author, the scientist who led the work. The paper builds on a question Bagchi's lab has followed for more than a decade: why does PVT1 travel with MYC? In 2014, from the University of Minnesota, Bagchi's group showed in Nature that cancers with extra copies of MYC also gain PVT1 and need it, because PVT1 keeps MYC protein stable. A 2016 paper showed MYC and PVT1 working together in breast cancer.

Bagchi trained at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory with Alea Mills. As first author of a 2007 Cell paper, Bagchi used chromosome engineering in mice, adding or deleting a large stretch of DNA matching human chromosome region 1p36, to identify the chromatin regulator CHD5 as a tumour suppressor that works through the p53 pathway.

Bagchi moved to Sanford Burnham Prebys in La Jolla, where the lab continues to engineer large genome rearrangements to find cancer genes and has discovered small proteins hidden in RNAs thought to be non-coding, including Firefox and, in a companion 2026 paper, Honeybadger, which restrains RAS-MAPK signalling. Bagchi also collaborates on brain tumour and pancreatic cancer studies at the institute.

studies.title: Firefox, a protein encoded by circular PVT1, is essential for MYC-driven oncogenesis.

story: Chang-Myung Oh is the senior author of SONH2026, with Hangyul Song as first author. The study looks at heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), in which the heart pumps a normal share of blood per beat but its muscle is stiff and fills poorly. Urolithin A, a compound that gut bacteria make from foods such as pomegranates, improved heart function and structure in HFpEF mice. It activated AMPK, the cell's energy sensor, turned down mTOR, and so restored mitophagy, the removal of damaged mitochondria. It also lowered blood ceramides, fatty molecules linked to heart damage, through changes in the gut microbiome. These findings come from mice and cell models.

PubMed lists more than seventy papers under this name with a GIST affiliation. No official profile page could be opened, so the title and training are not given here, and the position shown is the affiliation on the Atlas paper.

current.lab_name: Department of Molecular Medicine, Institute of Biotechnology, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
current.role: Molecular biologist at UT Health San Antonio who works on rapamycin and aging in mice, from the Interventions Testing Program lifespan studies to cancer prevention in tumour-prone mice
current.sub: Department of Molecular Medicine and Institute of Biotechnology, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio · Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies · Mays Cancer Center (PubMed affiliations to 2023)
story: Zelton Dave Sharp is a co-author of three Interventions Testing Program (ITP) papers in this Atlas. The ITP, funded by the US National Institute on Aging, tests possible anti-aging drugs in genetically mixed mice at three sites at once, so a result has to hold up in different labs. In HAR2009, rapamycin added to food from 600 days of age, already late in a mouse's life, extended both median and maximum lifespan in males and females. MIL2011 showed in the same design that rapamycin raised median lifespan by 10 to 18 percent while resveratrol and simvastatin had no effect. MIL2014 found that the gain depends on dose, is larger in females, and works differently from dietary restriction. These were the first convincing drug results for lifespan in mammals, but they are mouse results.

Sharp's own papers follow the same drug. As senior author, Sharp showed in 2013 that rapamycin lengthens the life of mice carrying one faulty copy of the Rb1 tumour suppressor gene by holding back their neuroendocrine tumours, and in 2016 described how mice adapt to long-term rapamycin. Sharp also co-authored a 2019 study linking mTORC1 to muscle fibre damage with age, and in 2023 was first author of a review in Experimental Gerontology calling rapamycin the only drug consistently shown to increase mammalian lifespan.

PubMed lists Sharp in the Department of Molecular Medicine and the Institute of Biotechnology at UT Health San Antonio, with links to the Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies and the Mays Cancer Center.

story: Epilepsy often develops over time after an injury or a series of seizures, a process called epileptogenesis. In the Atlas study MADKOUR2026, Mahmoud Elshal was last author, the position that usually marks the senior scientist who supervised the work. Rats received repeated small doses of PTZ, a chemical that lowers the seizure threshold, so that seizures grow stronger with each dose (kindling). Rats pre-treated with carvedilol, a common heart and blood-pressure drug, had lower seizure scores, less damage in the hippocampus, the memory region of the brain, and less inflammation driven by the NLRP3 inflammasome. Levels of PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway proteins changed at the same time. The authors state that these are associations and do not prove that mTOR signalling causes the benefit.

Elshal works in the Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology of the Faculty of Pharmacy at Mansoura University in Egypt. PubMed lists dozens of papers with this affiliation, most of them rodent studies that repurpose approved drugs. In 2026 the same team reported that empagliflozin, a diabetes drug, reduced PTZ-induced seizures in rats and strengthened the effect of the antiseizure drug levetiracetam, and a 2024 study in mice found that the diabetes drug sitagliptin protected the liver against chemically induced cholestasis, a blockage of bile flow. No official profile page was found.

studies.title: Carvedilol attenuates PTZ-induced epileptogenesis: associations with hippocampal neuroinflammation and PI3K/AKT/mTOR-related alterations.

story: Valérie Gailus-Durner is a co-author on two Atlas studies that relied on large-scale mouse phenotyping, the systematic measuring of many body functions in the same animals. EIS2016 showed that oral spermidine, a natural compound also found in food, lengthened the lives of mice, kept heart muscle from thickening and kept the heart able to relax normally between beats. The benefit disappeared in mice whose heart muscle cells lack the autophagy gene Atg5, so autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system, was needed for the effect. The paper also included a human diet survey linking spermidine intake to lower blood pressure and fewer heart problems, but that part is observational and cannot show cause. NEF2013 gave rapamycin, the drug that blocks mTOR, to young and old mice and measured a very wide panel of body functions. Rapamycin lengthened life but changed only a few of the classic signs of ageing, so a longer life did not mean that ageing slowed down across the whole body. Both are mouse studies.

Gailus-Durner works at the Institute of Experimental Genetics and German Mouse Clinic in Neuherberg, near Munich, and appears together with Helmut Fuchs and the institute director Martin Hrabě de Angelis on more than a hundred PubMed papers. The German Mouse Clinic at Helmholtz Munich tests mouse models in a standardised way across many organ systems; its recent papers cover heart size, movement, behaviour, metabolism and blood values. Recent examples are a 2026 study of how heart weight should be compared between mice of different sizes, using data from more than 25,000 animals, and a 2026 mouse model of KMT2B-related dystonia, a genetic movement disorder.

current.lab_name: Aylett Group, Section for Structural and Synthetic Biology, Department of Infectious Disease, Imperial College London (London, England, United Kingdom)
current.role: Structural biologist who solved the first cryo-EM architecture of human mTORC1 at ETH Zurich and now leads a cryo-EM group at Imperial College London
current.sub: Section for Structural and Synthetic Biology, Department of Infectious Disease, Imperial College London (papers 2020–2026) · Institute of Molecular Biology and Biophysics, ETH Zurich (papers 2015–2018) · MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge (2012 paper with Jan Löwe)
story: Christopher Aylett is first author of AYL2015, the first detailed 3D architecture of human mTORC1, made by cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). The structure showed that mTORC1 is a dimer, two copies of mTOR, Raptor and mLST8 joined into a lozenge-shaped complex with the two kinase active sites sitting in deep clefts. That arrangement explains how the complex limits which proteins can reach the active site, and how the drug pair rapamycin-FKBP12 narrows the entrance further. Aylett is also a co-author of STU2018, the matching architecture of the mTORC2 core.

Aylett's earlier work, at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge with Jan Löwe, was on bacterial proteins that push plasmids apart before cell division; a 2012 paper there described a DNA-protein filament at the heart of the TubZRC system. The mTOR structures came from a period at the Institute of Molecular Biology and Biophysics of ETH Zurich, working with Nenad Ban and Timm Maier.

Since about 2020 Aylett has led a group in the Section for Structural and Synthetic Biology of the Department of Infectious Disease at Imperial College London. The lab uses cryo-EM on large molecular machines, including the unusual RNA polymerase of the giant bacteriophage PhiKZ, a virus being explored as a treatment for Pseudomonas infections (2026), and develops simpler ways to prepare cryo-EM samples, such as a 3D-printed tool for moving fragile carbon and graphene support films.

story: Trevor Stitt is a co-author of two 2001 Atlas papers from Regeneron that made mTOR central to muscle biology. BOD2001 showed in living mice and rats that switching on Akt makes muscle fibres grow larger, that blocking mTOR with rapamycin stops this growth, and that active Akt can protect muscle from wasting (atrophy). ROM2001 showed in cultured muscle cells (myotubes) that the growth signal IGF-1 enlarges muscle cells through Akt and two branches below it, mTOR and GSK3. Together these papers explain why mTOR is the main switch linking growth signals and exercise to muscle size.

PubMed lists Stitt at Regeneron Pharmaceuticals in Tarrytown, New York, on 23 papers. The earlier ones come from Regeneron's work on growth factors and their receptors in the nervous system. Later papers stay with the muscle program led by David Glass, including a 2004 paper on how IGF-1 and Akt block the switching on of the atrophy enzymes MuRF1 and MAFbx, and a 2007 paper showing that MuRF1 breaks down myosin heavy chain, the main motor protein of muscle.

story: The lysosome is a small sac inside the cell that breaks down old proteins and organelles and stores the freed amino acids. It is also the platform where mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on. Sze Ham Chan is a co-author on two Atlas papers that looked inside lysosomes. In ABU2017, the team pulled lysosomes out of human cells within minutes and measured what was in them. When mTOR was blocked, most essential amino acids stopped leaving the lysosome, so the organelle became a store rather than a source. The study used one human cell line and short drug treatments.

In WYA2018, the same lysosome-isolation method was used to list 828 proteins that gather at lysosomes and to see which ones change when mTORC1 is switched off. One of them, NUFIP1, moved from the nucleus to autophagosomes and lysosomes and carried ribosomes there to be digested. This kind of self-eating of ribosomes, called ribophagy, gives a starving cell back amino acids and nucleotides. The work was done in human cells.

PubMed lists Chan at the Whitehead Institute on a series of papers from 2016 to 2023, including a 2016 Nature Chemical Biology study of a PHGDH inhibitor that blocks serine synthesis in cancer cells, the 2022 Nature paper that used a LysoTag mouse to show what the Batten disease gene CLN3 does in lysosomes, and a 2023 Cell Chemical Biology study showing that cancer cells respond differently to metabolic drugs when grown in a medium made from serum. The 2022 record also lists the Department of Pharmacology at the University of Virginia School of Medicine. No official profile page was found, so the current position could not be confirmed.

story: Bailey Knopf was first author of a 2026 review in Cell Press Blue (KNO2026) that asks what eating less protein does to an aging body. Across many organisms, cutting dietary protein, or only certain essential amino acids such as methionine, isoleucine and valine, improves metabolic health and can lengthen healthy life and lifespan. The review argues that the make-up of the protein, which amino acids it contains, matters as much as the amount, and that much of the effect runs through nutrient-sensing pathways, including mTORC1, the growth-control complex. Most of the evidence it summarises comes from animals.

Knopf is also a co-author of the Lamming lab's 2026 study on restricting single branched-chain amino acids in Alzheimer's model mice (BAB2025), in which cutting isoleucine or valine, but not leucine, improved metabolic health. PubMed lists about a dozen papers with Knopf's name since 2025, all from Lamming's group, including a 2025 preprint showing that the body's production of ketone bodies is not needed for the metabolic changes caused by calorie restriction in mice. No position beyond the Lamming lab could be confirmed.

current.role: Metabolism researcher in Vincent Giguère's laboratory at McGill who studies how the nuclear receptor ERR-alpha controls fat handling in the liver, including the fatty liver caused by rapamycin

story: Wafa B'chir was first author of a 2026 Journal of Endocrinology study (BCH2026) on a side effect of rapamycin. Rapamycin blocks mTORC1, the growth-control complex, and is used to prevent organ rejection. In mice it can also cause fatty liver, where fat builds up inside liver cells. The team added chloroquine, an old antimalarial drug, and found that it made the rapamycin-induced fatty liver milder. Measuring all the genes switched on in the liver showed that chloroquine undid much of rapamycin's push on fat-handling genes, and the nuclear receptor ERR-alpha, a master switch for energy metabolism, came out as a top controller. In mice lacking ERR-alpha, chloroquine no longer helped. This is a mouse study, and it does not show that the combination is safe or useful in patients.

B'chir came to this from nutrition and stress biology. In 2013, at the INRA Human Nutrition Unit in Clermont-Ferrand, France, B'chir was first author of a Nucleic Acids Research paper showing that when amino acids run out, the GCN2 and PERK stress kinases act through ATF4 and CHOP to switch on a whole set of autophagy genes. At McGill's Goodman Cancer Research Centre B'chir moved to the liver: a 2018 first-author paper in Endocrinology found that mice without ERR-alpha are protected from fatty liver on a high-fat diet but cannot clear fat from the liver normally when fed again after fasting.
B'chir has continued with the Giguère group at the Goodman Cancer Institute on work about ERR-alpha in the heart (2022) and in the progression of fatty liver to liver inflammation in mice (2023).

current.lab_name: Phillips Lab, Institute of Ecology and Evolution, University of Oregon (Eugene, Oregon, USA)
current.role: Worm biologist in Patrick Phillips' lab at the University of Oregon who studies how ageing differs between the sexes, using male C. elegans
current.sub: Institute of Ecology and Evolution, University of Oregon (Patrick Phillips lab, papers 2025–2026) · Department of Biology, Syracuse University (Sarah Hall lab, 2026 paper)
story: Rose Al-Saadi is first author of ALS2026, a study in the tiny roundworm C. elegans. Most worm ageing research uses hermaphrodites, which make both eggs and sperm; this study looked at males. The team used a chemical switch (auxin-inducible degradation) to destroy DAF-2, the worm's insulin/IGF-1 receptor, throughout the body of adult males. Median lifespan rose by more than 440 percent, one of the largest lifespan gains reported for a single intervention, and the males stayed able to mate much later in life. Destroying DAF-2 only in the male germline, in contrast, shortened life, the opposite of what happens in hermaphrodites.

The insulin/IGF-1 pathway and mTOR are linked growth signals that both control ageing, so the paper shows that the sexes can respond differently to the same anti-ageing switch. The results are in worms and need testing in other animals.

Al-Saadi works with Patrick Phillips at the Institute of Ecology and Evolution of the University of Oregon on sex differences in ageing. A 2026 GeroScience paper from the pair tested seven compounds known to extend hermaphrodite lifespan: all lengthened male life, but only sulforaphane and metformin also kept males reproductively fit late in life. Earlier work in Sarah Hall's lab at Syracuse University, published in 2026, showed that a male worm's developmental history, including passage through the stress-resistant dauer stage, shapes how often worms cross-mate. No personal profile page was found, so the job title is not confirmed.

studies.title: Disruption of the insulin/IGF-1 signaling pathway in Caenorhabditis elegans dramatically increases male longevity and enhances reproductive health late in life

current.sub: State Key Laboratory of Membrane Biology and Beijing Advanced Innovation Center for Structural Biology, School of Life Sciences, Tsinghua University (affiliation on PubMed papers)
story: Jian Yin is the first author of YIN2026, a structural study of PAT1 (also called SLC36A1), a human transporter that carries small amino acids across membranes together with protons. Earlier work by other groups had shown that PAT1 sits on lysosomes, the cell's recycling compartments, and helps move amino acids out of them, which affects how mTORC1, the cell's nutrient sensor, is switched on. Yin and colleagues used cryo-electron microscopy, a method that freezes proteins and images them with electrons, to see PAT1 empty and with different amino acids bound. The structures show that the transporter grips many different amino acids in a similar way. The study is about the shape and mechanism of the protein; the mTORC1 link comes from the earlier work.

PubMed lists Yin at Tsinghua University's School of Life Sciences on about a dozen structural papers on membrane transporters, most of them with M. Yang as senior author, from the State Key Laboratory of Membrane Biology and the Beijing Advanced Innovation Center for Structural Biology.
Because Yin is a common surname, only papers from this Tsinghua structural biology group were counted. No official profile was found, so training and position are not given.

studies.title: Substrate recognition and transport mechanism of the human proton-coupled amino-acid transporter 1 (SLC36A1)

current.lab_name: Center for Regenerative Sciences and Department of Comprehensive Dentistry, School of Dentistry, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
current.role: Oral biology researcher at the UT Health San Antonio School of Dentistry who works on dental caries, oral biofilms and salivary gland ageing, and first author of the marmoset study of rapamycin and the ageing salivary gland
current.sub: Center for Regenerative Sciences and Department of Comprehensive Dentistry, School of Dentistry, UT Health San Antonio (papers 2023–2026)
story: Older people often have a dry mouth because their salivary glands shrink and scar. In the Atlas study ABD2026, Abdul-Azees, Chih-Ko Yeh and colleagues looked at the submandibular salivary gland of the common marmoset, a small primate that ages much faster than humans. Older glands had fewer of the cells that make saliva, more duct and scar-like connective tissue, more fat build-up and more dying and senescent (permanently arrested) cells. Marmosets given rapamycin by mouth for a long period kept more of the saliva-making structure and showed less scarring and fat build-up.

Rapamycin blocks mTORC1, the growth-control complex. The study suggests that some age-related damage in a primate gland can be slowed by this drug. It was a tissue study in a small number of animals and was not tested in people.

On PubMed, Abdul-Azees first appears in 2023 in Bennett Amaechi's group in the Department of Comprehensive Dentistry at UT Health San Antonio, on a laboratory model of tooth decay (an artificial mouth) and later on toothpaste formulas that prevent caries. Since 2025 the papers carry the Center for Regenerative Sciences affiliation with Chih-Ko Yeh and Xiao-Dong Chen, including work on how bacterial biofilms grow on dental filling materials.

studies.title: Rapamycin Attenuates Age-Related Changes in Marmoset Submandibular Gland: A Non-Human Primate Model of Human Oral Aging.

current.lab_name: Grewal Lab, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Cumming School of Medicine, University of Calgary (Calgary, Alberta, Canada)
current.role: Fruit fly biologist in Savraj Grewal's Calgary lab who studies how growth signals and mitochondria in one tissue control how fast the whole larva grows
current.sub: Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Clark H. Smith Brain Tumour Centre and Arnie Charbonneau Cancer Institute, University of Calgary (papers with Savraj Grewal, 2018–2026)
story: Shrivani Sriskanthadevan-Pirahas is the first author of the Atlas study SRI2026, from Savraj Grewal's lab at the University of Calgary. The work was done in fruit fly (Drosophila) larvae. Their fat body senses food and tells the rest of the body how fast to grow. The study found that TOR, the nutrient-sensing growth kinase, keeps the protein TFAM low in the fat body. TFAM switches on the genes inside mitochondria, the cell's power plants. TOR acts on TFAM after its message is made, and this link in one tissue helps set the growth rate of the whole animal. It is a fly study and shows a mechanism, not a result in people.

The PubMed record shows a steady path in the same lab. In 2018 Sriskanthadevan-Pirahas was first author of two papers showing that the Ras/ERK growth pathway drives fly growth by boosting the cell's protein-making machinery: tRNA synthesis through the repressor Maf1, and ribosomal RNA synthesis through the factor TIF-IA. In 2022, in Cell Reports, the same team showed that lowering mitochondrial energy production only in the fat body made larvae grow faster, by reducing secreted signals that hold back insulin. A 2023 paper extended the idea to macrophage-like blood cells.
All of these papers list the University of Calgary. No separate official profile was found, so the current position is given as the affiliation on the Atlas paper.

studies.title: Nutrient/TOR signaling controls adipose mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) to regulate organismal growth in Drosophila

current.lab_name: Jie Wang group, Department of Chemistry, Southern University of Science and Technology (Shenzhen, China)
current.role: Chemical biologist at SUSTech in Shenzhen who used a light-activated methionine probe to identify PKM2 as a methionine sensor for mTORC1
current.sub: Department of Chemistry, Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Catalysis and State Key Laboratory of Medical Proteomics, Southern University of Science and Technology (2026, at the time of the study)
story: Zixin Sang is first author of the Atlas study SANG2026, from Jie Wang's group in the Department of Chemistry at the Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech) in Shenzhen. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, only runs when amino acids are available, and cells have dedicated sensor proteins that report each amino acid. For methionine the known sensor, SAMTOR, does not read methionine itself but a product made from it, S-adenosylmethionine (SAM). Whether any protein reads free methionine directly was an open question.

Sang and colleagues built a "Trojan" methionine: a copy of the amino acid that cells take up normally but that carries a chemical group which, when hit with light, links the probe to whatever protein is holding it. Fishing out these proteins with chemoproteomics, a method that identifies protein targets of small molecules on a large scale, pointed to PKM2. PKM2 is best known as a glycolysis enzyme, but here it bound methionine through a separate pocket, independently of its enzyme activity, and passed the signal to mTORC1 through the GATOR2 complex. The work was done in cultured cells and complements SAMTOR rather than replacing it.

PubMed lists Sang at the Department of Chemistry, Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Catalysis and State Key Laboratory of Medical Proteomics at SUSTech. No other papers or an official page could be tied to this person, so the profile rests on this study.

studies.title: "Trojan" Methionine Probe Reveals PKM2 as a Methionine-Sensing Protein in the mTORC1 Pathway

previous_note: Only one paper; career stage (student or postdoc) not confirmed.

current.lab_name: Bai Lab, Department of Medical Chemistry, Faculty of Medicine, University of Debrecen (Debrecen, Hungary)
current.role: Researcher in Péter Bai's group at the University of Debrecen who studies how ADP-ribosylating enzymes control fat cell development through AMPK and mTOR
current.sub: Department of Medical Chemistry, Faculty of Medicine, University of Debrecen (papers 2019–2026)
story: Fat cells form from precursor cells in a process called adipocyte differentiation, which needs mTORC1, the growth-control complex, to be active. In RAUCH2026, Boglarka Rauch and colleagues in Péter Bai's group worked on tankyrases, enzymes that attach chains of ADP-ribose to other proteins and so change how those proteins behave. In a cell line, deleting tankyrase-1 or tankyrase-2 slowed fat cell formation. The cells showed active AMPK, the energy sensor, low mTORC1 activity and blocked autophagy. The defect caused by losing tankyrase-2 could be fixed by NV-5138, a drug that switches mTORC1 on, or by blocking LKB1, the kinase that activates AMPK. Tankyrase-2 was found to ADP-ribosylate LKB1, which suggests that it normally keeps the LKB1-AMPK brake on mTORC1 in check. The findings come from cultured cells only.

Rauch has published with the Bai group in the Department of Medical Chemistry at the University of Debrecen since 2019, including a 2023 screen of bacterial metabolites for effects on breast cancer cell growth. No personal institutional page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

studies.title: Tankyrase-2 regulates adipocyte differentiation through AMPK/mTOR signaling.

current.lab_name: Department of Neurosurgery, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus (Aurora, Colorado, USA)
current.role: Neuroscience researcher and first author of a 2026 spatial study of the human hippocampus in Down syndrome with Alzheimer's disease, which found mTOR and insulin signalling disturbed in specific cell layers
current.sub: Department of Neurosurgery, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Almost everyone with Down syndrome has an extra copy of the amyloid precursor protein gene on chromosome 21, and Alzheimer's disease changes in the brain are common as they age. Abigail Nordbeck's 2026 study, with Ann-Charlotte Granholm as senior author, examined post-mortem hippocampus, the brain region central to forming memories, from people with Down syndrome and Alzheimer's neuropathology.

The team combined spatial transcriptomics, which measures gene activity while keeping its location in the tissue, with localized proteomics, which measures proteins in small chosen regions. mTOR pathway signalling was significantly altered in particular hippocampal subfields, and insulin pathway signalling was altered mainly in dentate granule neurons. In other words, the disturbance is local and cell-type specific rather than spread evenly through the tissue. The authors present these as preliminary observations in human tissue; they show associations and cannot say whether the changes cause the disease or follow from it.
PubMed lists Nordbeck at the Department of Neurosurgery of the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus for this study. A current position could not be confirmed from an official page.

studies.title: Disruption of hippocampal upstream regulators of mTOR and insulin pathways in Down syndrome with Alzheimer's disease neuropathology: Preliminary observations

current.lab_name: Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology, Faculty of Pharmacy, Mansoura University (Mansoura, Egypt)
current.role: Pharmacologist at Mansoura University who tests approved drugs as protection against seizures and kidney injury in rats
current.sub: Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology, Faculty of Pharmacy, Mansoura University (papers 2022–2026) · Faculty of Health Science Technology, Mansoura National University (2026)
story: Ahmed Madkour was first author of the Atlas study MADKOUR2026 in Scientific Reports, which asked whether carvedilol, a beta-blocker used for heart failure and high blood pressure, could slow the development of epilepsy. Rats received repeated doses of PTZ, a chemical that makes seizures easier to trigger, until seizures became stronger over time (kindling). Rats given carvedilol beforehand had lower seizure scores, less damage in the hippocampus and less inflammation linked to the NLRP3 inflammasome, an alarm system of immune cells. Proteins of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, which controls cell growth and survival, changed at the same time. The authors say the study shows associations only, so it does not prove that mTOR signalling is the reason carvedilol helped.

PubMed lists Madkour at the Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology of the Faculty of Pharmacy at Mansoura University, Egypt, from 2022 onward. An earlier first-author paper (2022) found that lactoferrin, an iron-binding milk protein, protected rat kidneys in a dose-dependent way after muscle breakdown caused by glycerol. A 2026 first-author paper in Neurotoxicology, again with Mahmoud Elshal, reported that the diabetes drug empagliflozin reduced PTZ-induced seizures in rats and worked best together with a lower dose of levetiracetam. That paper also lists the Faculty of Health Science Technology at Mansoura National University. No official profile page was found.

studies.title: Carvedilol attenuates PTZ-induced epileptogenesis: associations with hippocampal neuroinflammation and PI3K/AKT/mTOR-related alterations.

current.lab_name: Department of Urology, Taizhou Hospital of Zhejiang Province, Wenzhou Medical University (Taizhou, China)
current.role: Urologist in Zhejiang who works with colleagues on inherited endocrine tumour syndromes and wrote a review re-examining how FLCN loss changes mTORC1 signalling in Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome
current.sub: Department of Urology, Taizhou Hospital of Zhejiang Province, affiliated to Wenzhou Medical University (2026) · Department of Urology / Oncologic and Urologic Surgery, 903rd PLA Hospital, Hangzhou Medical College (2023–2025)
story: Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome is an inherited condition caused by faults in the FLCN gene. People with it can get benign skin bumps, air-filled cysts in the lungs that may cause a collapsed lung, and kidney tumours. For years the explanation was simple: lose FLCN and mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on everywhere. In a 2026 review in Frontiers in Oncology (CAO2026), Zhi-Lie Cao, first author, with Wei-Ying Chen as senior author, argues that this picture does not fit the evidence. FLCN acts on the RagC/D switch proteins, which control only some mTORC1 targets, above all the MiT/TFE transcription factors. Losing both copies of FLCN lets these factors pile up in the nucleus and drives kidney tumours, while losing one copy may be enough for lung and skin changes. As a review, it reports no new experiments.

PubMed shows Cao as a urologist. In 2023 and 2025 papers the address is the urology and oncologic surgery department of the 903rd PLA Hospital of Hangzhou Medical College; by 2026 it is the Department of Urology of Taizhou Hospital of Zhejiang Province, affiliated to Wenzhou Medical University. With Chen and Xiao-Ping Qi, Cao has co-authored case reports and literature reviews on rare tumours, including a primary seminoma of the prostate (2023) and families with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A caused by RET mutations (2025, 2026). No official profile page was found.

studies.title: Substrate-selective mTORC1 regulation and gene dosage-dependent tissue divergence in Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome

current.lab_name: Albeck Lab, Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, University of California, Davis (Davis, California, USA)
current.role: Quantitative cell biologist trained in John Albeck's lab at UC Davis, who used live single-cell imaging to show that the mTORC1-TFEB signalling axis tracks nutrients and growth factors continuously
current.sub: Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, University of California, Davis (Albeck lab, papers 2015–2023, at the time of the study)
story: Breanne Sparta was first author of a 2023 eLife paper in this Atlas (SPA2023). Most experiments on mTORC1, the growth-control complex, grind up millions of cells and measure an average at a few time points. This study filmed single living human breast epithelial cells (MCF10A) carrying fluorescent reporters, and followed TFEB, a regulator of lysosomes and autophagy that mTORC1 holds outside the nucleus, together with AMPK and AKT activity. mTORC1-TFEB signalling adjusted smoothly to amino acids and insulin whether they were given alone, one after the other or together. At normal body levels of amino acids the three signals rose and fell in step, and these graded changes tracked how fast the cells were making protein. The results come from one cultured cell line.

Sparta's earlier work in Albeck's lab also used live-cell reporters. As first author of a 2015 Journal of Biological Chemistry paper, Sparta showed that pulses of ERK activity triggered by the growth factor EGF depend on mechanisms at the receptor. Sparta co-authored a 2017 methods chapter on imaging ERK signalling with fluorescent biosensors, a 2017 modelling study of oscillations in MAPK signalling, and a 2021 Cell Metabolism paper on how single cells pass through temporary phases of resistance to drugs that block mitochondrial energy production. Sparta's current position could not be confirmed.

studies.title: Continuous sensing of nutrients and growth factors by the mTORC1-TFEB axis
